weekLabel: Week 10 · Meeting A · Optimization I: Formulation and Linear Solvers

slides.title: Formulate a linear model, then solve it with a global guarantee
slides.subtitle: Design variables, objectives, constraints, bounds, feasible regions, and numerical tolerances
slides.teaching: Ask whether a solver's success flag is enough. Today separates the mathematical LP guarantee from the finite tolerances used by numerical software.

slides.title: Formulate before you decide
slides.statement: A real optimization problem is stated in variables, an objective, and constraints — not chosen by gut feeling.
slides.supporting: Radley Hall's roof: an 'obvious' all-solar strategy earns $7,200/yr; an 'obvious' all-green strategy earns $5,000/yr. Today's formulated-and-solved answer earns $7,800/yr — beating both.
slides.teaching: Do not reveal the winning mix yet — just the three numbers. Let students sit with the fact that neither pure guess wins.

outcomes.head: Define
outcomes.body: Name the design variables, objective function, constraints, and bounds for a real design decision.

outcomes.head: Formulate
outcomes.body: Write a linear program in the standard form every solver expects.

outcomes.head: Explain
outcomes.body: State the LP theorem correctly: if a finite optimum exists, at least one optimal extreme point exists; an entire edge or face can also be optimal.

outcomes.head: Compare
outcomes.body: Show a formulated-and-solved answer beating both 'obvious' naive strategies, with every constraint hand-verified.

slides.teaching: Name this explicitly as algorithm family #1 of three the course teaches — Week 11 (gradient search) and Week 12 (heuristic search) are the other two.

items: Optimization has three algorithm families - today starts with the exact one
Vocabulary: design variables, objective function, constraints, bounds
The feasible region and standard form, made geometric
Why linear = exact: simplex and interior-point, solved live on Radley Hall's roof
slides.teaching: Tell students the whole arc ends with the identical roof problem solved twice, by two different exact algorithms, with the identical answer — that repetition is deliberate.

slides.title: Optimization has three algorithm families — this course teaches all three
rows: a global LP optimum, subject to feasibility, boundedness, and tolerances
slides.callout: Linear programming has the strongest guarantee in this sequence, but a solver still reports a numerical solution to stated feasibility and optimality tolerances.
slides.teaching: Write all three method names on the board now — students will see linprog today, minimize in two weeks, and a genetic algorithm the week after that.

slides.title: Formulation connects four different kinds of information

steps.label: VARIABLES
steps.head: What may change?
steps.body: x1 = solar area and x2 = green-roof area, both in m².

steps.label: OBJECTIVE
steps.head: What ranks designs?
steps.body: Annual benefit combines 60x1 + 25x2 into one quantity.

steps.label: CONSTRAINTS
steps.head: What must hold?
steps.body: Total area and installed cost limit the candidate set.

steps.label: BOUNDS
steps.head: What is meaningful?
steps.body: Nonnegative areas and the solar structural cap define variable limits.

slides.teaching: Use the diagram as the overview; the following slides define each piece. Ask which node would change if a skylight became a third choice.

slides.title: Design variable, defined
slides.definition: A design variable is a quantity your formulation is free to choose — the 'moving part' the solver adjusts to search for the best answer. Every other piece (objective, constraints, bounds) is written IN TERMS OF the design variables, so naming them, with units, is always step one.

example.head: x1 = solar area (m2), x2 = green roof area (m2)
example.body: Radley Hall's roof allocation has exactly two design variables. Every formula that follows — the objective, both constraints, and the bounds — is written only in terms of x1 and x2; nothing else is allowed to vary.

slides.note: A design variable is not the same as a fixed input like the $60/m2 benefit rate — that is a parameter, a number you plug in. A design variable is a number the solver itself is free to change.
slides.teaching: Name x1 and x2 explicitly before the objective/constraint/bounds slides that follow — every one of them is written only in terms of these two variables.

slides.title: Objective function, defined
slides.definition: The single number you are trying to maximize or minimize, written as a formula in the design variables. Optimization always needs exactly one objective — one number to rank every candidate design by.

example.head: maximize 60x1 + 25x2
example.body: Solar returns $60/m2/yr; green roof returns $25/m2/yr. Solar earns more per m2 — so why not go all-solar? Constraints, next, are why.

slides.note: Real projects often care about cost AND daylight AND embodied carbon at once — but linprog needs those combined into ONE formula (or solved as separate scenarios), never several objectives at the same time.
slides.teaching: Let the 60 vs. 25 per-m2 gap sit visibly for a moment — it is exactly the trap the naive 'all-solar' strategy falls into.

slides.title: Constraint, defined
slides.definition: A hard limit the design must satisfy, written as an inequality (<=, >=) or an equality (=) in the design variables. A design that violates even one constraint is not a candidate design at all.

example.head: x1 + x2 <= 200
example.body: Area: x1 + x2 <= 200 (only 200 m2 of roof exists). Budget: 400x1 + 150x2 <= 50,000 (solar installs at $400/m2, green roof at $150/m2; the board approved $50,000).

slides.note: A constraint links TWO OR MORE variables together (like x1 + x2 <= 200). A bound, next slide, limits only ONE variable by itself — that difference is why linprog asks for them as separate arguments.
slides.teaching: Point out both constraints are straight lines (linear) in x1, x2 — that fact is what makes today's problem solvable exactly, foreshadowed here.

slides.title: Bounds, defined
slides.definition: Bounds are simple lower/upper limits on ONE variable at a time, written lb <= x <= ub. Bounds are technically a special case of constraints, but scipy.optimize.linprog asks for them separately because they are so common.

example.head: bounds = [(0, 120), (0, None)]
example.body: Solar is structurally capped at 120 m2 — the existing roof structure cannot support panels everywhere: 0 <= x1 <= 120. Green roof has no extra upper bound beyond what area and budget already limit: x2 >= 0.

slides.note: 'None' as an upper bound means 'no extra limit here' — not zero and not infinity as a number. x2 is still limited indirectly by the area and budget constraints.
slides.teaching: Ask why a negative area would be meaningless before revealing x >= 0 — ties bounds back to real-world sense-checking, not arbitrary math.

slides.title: Feasible region, defined
slides.definition: The feasible region is the set of every (x1, x2) pair that satisfies ALL constraints and bounds at once. Optimizing means searching only inside this region for the best objective value — never outside it.

example.head: A five-sided flat polygon
example.body: Radley Hall's feasible region, shown on the next chart: every point inside or on its edge is a legal roof design; every point outside breaks the area limit, the budget, or the structural cap.

slides.note: The region's EDGE counts as feasible, not just its interior — a design using the roof's full 200 m2 exactly (on the boundary) is just as legal as one using only 150 m2 (inside).
slides.teaching: Ask students to name one (x1,x2) pair they are confident is OUTSIDE the feasible region before the chart reveals its shape (e.g., (150,100) breaks both area and the solar bound).

slides.title: Checking a candidate point against every constraint
slides.callout: Limits: area <= 200 m2 total; budget <= $50,000. Only two of these four candidates satisfy both — the true optimum (found later) sits at exactly one of the feasible corners.
slides.teaching: Have students check each candidate against BOTH constraints by hand before revealing the feasible? column — (100,100) is the one most students miss, since it looks 'reasonable' but breaks the budget.

slides.title: The feasible region is a flat-sided polygon
slides.chartTitle: Radley Hall roof: feasible (x1, x2) region
slides.explainHead: Every straight edge is one constraint
slides.explainBody: Bottom edge: x2 = 0. Right edge: x1 = 120 (the structural bound). Upper-right edge: the $50,000 budget line. Upper-left edge: the 200 m2 area line. Every edge of this polygon is exactly one constraint or bound holding with equality — that is what makes it flat-sided, not curved.
slides.teaching: Trace each of the four edges with a finger while naming which constraint or bound drew it. This flat-sided shape is the direct geometric consequence of every constraint being linear.

slides.title: Vertex, defined
slides.definition: A vertex (extreme point) is where feasible-region edges meet. If a linear program has a finite optimum, at least one optimal solution occurs at an extreme point. The optimum need not be unique: a whole edge or face can share the same objective value.

example.head: Five vertices in this worked instance
example.body: Checking the five vertices reveals one unique winner here. In a different LP, parallel objective contours can make every point on an edge optimal.

slides.note: Do not reverse the theorem: it guarantees that at least one optimal vertex exists, not that every optimum is a vertex or that every LP has a unique solution.
slides.teaching: Point back at the candidate-check table: (50,50) was feasible but is NOT a vertex — only the five corners qualify.

slides.title: Predict which limits bind, which have slack
slides.code:
A_ub = [[1, 1],       # area <= 200
        [400, 150]]   # budget <= 50000
b_ub = [200, 50000]
bounds = [(0, 120), (0, None)]  # structural cap on x1
slides.question: Which limits bind exactly, and which have slack?
slides.why: Area used = 200 and budget used = $50,000 — both at their limits, so both bind. The structural cap has slack: solar stays under 120 m2.
slides.teaching: Take a vote on all five options before revealing — the structural-cap distractor is the one most students pick, since it was introduced early and sounds important; it turns out not to bind at all.

slides.title: This worked LP has a unique optimal corner
slides.callout: Five corners, one winner in this instance: (80, 120) at $7,800/yr. If the objective were parallel to a binding edge, multiple points on that edge could tie.
slides.teaching: Have students compute at least one row's benefit by hand (e.g., 60*120 = 7200) before revealing the printed value. This table IS the fundamental theorem of linear programming, shown as five arithmetic facts instead of a proof.

slides.title: What the LP theorem guarantees
slides.statement: If a linear program has a finite optimum, at least one optimal solution is an extreme point of the feasible region.
slides.supporting: That supports a global guarantee for the mathematical model. A software solver still decides feasibility and optimality with numerical tolerances, and more than one solution may be optimal.
slides.teaching: Connect back to the vertex table: five corners were enough to find the guaranteed-best point of the entire continuous (x1, x2) plane, which has infinitely many points.

slides.title: Standard form, defined

left.head: Definition
left.body:
Standard form restates any linear program the same fixed way every solver expects:
minimize c^T x
subject to A_ub x <= b_ub
and lb <= x <= ub
c, A_ub, b_ub, lb, ub are just numbers arranged as vectors/matrices — no new math, just a fixed shape to fill in.

right.head: Why 'minimize', not 'maximize'
right.body: scipy.optimize.linprog only minimizes. To maximize 60x1 + 25x2, minimize its NEGATIVE, -60x1 — 25x2, instead — so c = [-60, -25]. Whatever x minimizes -f(x) also maximizes f(x).

slides.teaching: Write the general standard-form template on the board, then immediately fill in Radley Hall's numbers next to it — the mapping from words to arrays is today's real skill.

slides.title: linprog, defined

left.head: Definition
left.body: scipy.optimize.linprog(c, A_ub, b_ub, bounds) solves a linear program and returns a globally optimal numerical solution when the model is feasible and bounded, subject to solver tolerances. Unlike Week 11's minimize, no user-supplied starting guess is required.

right.head: What it returns
right.body:
res.x — the optimal design variables
res.fun — the minimized objective (negate it back for a maximize problem)
res.success / res.message — whether a feasible optimum was actually found

slides.teaching: Underline 'no starting guess required' — this is the single biggest procedural difference from Week 11's minimize, worth flagging now so it lands harder in two weeks.

slides.title: Translate the formulation into standard-form arrays
slides.code:
from scipy.optimize import linprog

# maximize 60*x1 + 25*x2  ->  minimize the negative
c = [-60, -25]
A_ub = [[1, 1],       # area:   x1 + x2 <= 200
        [400, 150]]   # budget: 400x1 + 150x2 <= 50000
b_ub = [200, 50000]
bounds = [(0, 120),   # solar: structural cap
          (0, None)]  # green roof: no extra bound
slides.explainHead: Four arrays, one per formulation piece
slides.explainBody: c holds the (negated) objective coefficients; A_ub/b_ub together encode both <= constraints as one matrix and one limit vector; bounds holds the per-variable limits. Nothing has been solved yet — this cell only reshapes the formulation into what linprog expects.
slides.teaching: Point at each array and name which formulation piece (objective, constraints, bounds) it holds. The next slide zooms into the actual solver call before it is run.

slides.title: linprog's call, argument by argument

parts.label: Inequality coefficients
parts.body: Left-hand-side numbers of every <= constraint, one row each.

parts.label: Per-variable limits
parts.body: Simple lb <= x <= ub pairs, one per design variable.

slides.teaching: Walk left to right: c is what to minimize, A_ub/b_ub are the two <= constraints as arrays, bounds are the per-variable limits. Predict the answer next, before the following slide reveals it.

slides.title: Which corner will linprog actually return?
slides.code:
res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
              bounds=bounds, method='highs')
print(res.x)
slides.question: Which vertex will res.x land on?
slides.why: (80, 120) earns $7,800/yr, the highest of the five vertices — and the theorem guarantees the optimum sits at one of them.
slides.teaching: Take a vote before revealing — most students can already reason this out from the vertex table two slides back. This is a genuine prediction, not a blind guess: they have every number needed already.

slides.title: Solved to tolerance, then verified
slides.code:
res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
              bounds=bounds, method='highs')
# 'highs' = scipy's default exact solver, explained next
print(res.x)
print(-res.fun)
slides.explainHead: One call, a globally optimal LP solution
slides.explainBody: The solver reports 80 m² solar, 120 m² green roof, and $7,800/yr. Treat the printed decimals as a numerical result: check res.success, residuals, and constraints with a tolerance before communicating the design.
slides.teaching: Run this live if possible. Confirm it matches your prediction from the last slide before revealing -res.fun. Verified against real scipy 1.17.1.

slides.title: Formulating and solving beats the two 'obvious' strategies
slides.callout: Neither pure strategy wins. $7,800/yr beats the better naive guess by $600/yr, and beats the other by $2,800/yr — purely from formulating and solving instead of guessing.
slides.teaching: Ask which naive strategy students would have picked before seeing this table — most guess all-solar, since it has the higher per-m2 return. The mixed answer is the whole lesson.

slides.title: Simplex, defined

left.head: Definition
left.body: The simplex family moves among basic feasible solutions (geometric corners) while improving the objective, using termination tests rather than literal exact arithmetic.

right.head: Why that is enough
right.body: For a feasible, bounded LP, simplex can establish a global optimum to numerical tolerances. Degeneracy and multiple optima mean the path and returned optimal point need not be unique.

slides.teaching: Sketch the walk on the feasible-region chart: (0,0) -> (120,0) -> (120,13.3) -> (80,120), improving at every step, stopping because (0,200) is worse.

slides.title: Interior-point, defined

left.head: Definition
left.body: An interior-point method moves through the feasible region toward optimality; production solvers may then use crossover to return a basic solution.

right.head: Same guarantee, different path
right.body: HiGHS provides deterministic LP algorithms with global guarantees for the model, reported to feasibility and optimality tolerances. Different algorithms may return different points on the same optimal face.

slides.teaching: Reassure students they do not need to choose a method by default — 'highs' picks one — but that method='highs-ds' or 'highs-ipm' exist if they want to force a specific one, shown next.

slides.title: Simplex pivots are non-decreasing — not always strict
slides.chartTitle: Radley Hall roof: an illustrative simplex path across the feasible region
slides.explainBody: The shown path visits the origin, (120,0), (120,13.33), and (80,120): three moves across four vertices. Benefit is non-decreasing here: $0 -> $7,200 -> $7,533 -> $7,800. In general, a degenerate simplex pivot can be flat, so 'strictly improves at every pivot' is too strong.
slides.teaching: Trace this as an illustrative corner path, naming the benefit at each visited vertex; do not claim HiGHS exposes or must follow this exact internal route. Interior-point methods instead approach an optimum through the feasible region's interior.

slides.title: Two algorithms agree on this instance
slides.code:
for method in ['highs-ds', 'highs-ipm']:
    res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
                   bounds=bounds, method=method)
    print(method, res.x, -res.fun)
slides.explainHead: Agreement is evidence, not a uniqueness theorem
slides.explainBody: Dual simplex and the interior-point method both return (80, 120), $7,800 for this LP. Other valid LPs can have multiple optimal points, and different algorithms may return different members of the same optimal edge or face.
slides.teaching: This is the sharpest possible contrast to set up for Week 11: there, changing the starting guess changes the answer. Here, changing the entire algorithm changes nothing.

slides.title: Package the whole workflow in one documented function
slides.code:
from scipy.optimize import linprog

def solve_roof_allocation(area_limit_m2: float,
                          budget_usd: float) -> dict:
    """Solve one roof scenario; check both limits."""
    c = [-60, -25]  # maximize -> minimize -60x1-25x2
    A_ub = [[1, 1], [400, 150]]  # area row, cost row
    b_ub = [area_limit_m2, budget_usd]
    bounds = [(0, 120), (0, None)]  # solar cap 120
    res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
                  bounds=bounds, method='highs')
    x1, x2 = res.x
    area_used = x1 + x2
    cost_used = 400 * x1 + 150 * x2
slides.explainHead: Formulate, solve, and verify — in one place
slides.explainBody: Everything from the last several slides now lives inside one function, in order: the four standard-form arrays, the linprog call, and the two quantities you would otherwise hand-check. Only what changes between scenarios becomes a parameter — area_limit_m2 and budget_usd; the $400/$150 install costs and the 120 m2 structural cap stay fixed inside. The docstring and type hints are the Week 4 convention: a reader learns what goes in and what comes back without running it.
slides.teaching: Point at each line and name which earlier slide it came from: c and A_ub/b_ub/bounds from the standard-form slide, linprog from the solve slide, area_used and cost_used from the vertex table's own arithmetic. Then ask why the $400/m2 install cost is NOT a parameter — because nothing in this problem ever changes it, while the approved budget plainly does.

slides.title: ...continued: return the answer and both constraint checks
slides.explainHead: A dict carries the answer AND its proof
slides.explainBody: The returned dict holds five facts, not one: both areas, the annual benefit (already negated back into a positive dollar figure), and whether each of the two constraints binds exactly. Because the checks travel with the answer, no caller can read solar_m2 without also seeing area_binds. Two scenarios, two lines of output, one function: at the approved $50,000 the split is 80/120 for $7,800/yr, and at $40,000 it shifts to 40/160 for $6,400/yr — both times spending every m2 and every dollar.
slides.teaching: Ask what would have to change to test a third budget — one more number in the list on the for line. That is the whole payoff: the formulation was written once and audited once, then reused. Verified against real scipy 1.17.1.

slides.title: Exact today; searched starting next week
slides.statement: A linear objective and linear constraints are what make an exact answer possible.
slides.supporting: The moment either the objective or a constraint curves — Week 11's territory — the corner guarantee disappears, and the computer must search from a starting guess instead.
slides.teaching: Name Week 11 explicitly here — students should leave today knowing exactly which problems get this shortcut and which do not.

slides.title: Project 2 needs this, not just today's lesson
slides.statement: linprog is one of two REQUIRED solvers for Project 2 Part II — the other, minimize, is Week 11's lesson.
slides.supporting: Whatever your own Project 2 problem is, if any part of it is linear in its design variables, formulate and solve that part with linprog exactly as done here — naming variables, writing the objective and constraints, and hand-verifying every constraint, exactly as Meeting B's studio requires.
slides.teaching: Name Project 2 Part II explicitly — both linprog (today) and minimize (Week 11) are required components of that assignment, not optional alternatives to pick between.

slides.title: Predict, then check, from the vertex table
slides.prompt: Before looking back, which of the five corners do you predict gives the highest annual benefit?
steps: State your predicted corner and why, out loud, before checking.
Look back at the vertex table shown earlier this deck.
Name the exact benefit at your predicted corner vs. the true best.
Name the TWO constraints that bind exactly at (80, 120).
slides.teaching: Most students guess (120,0) or (120,13.3), since solar has the higher per-m2 return — use the miss to reinforce that per-unit return alone cannot decide a constrained problem.

slides.title: Transfer the formulation: allocate an insulation budget
slides.prompt: Radley Hall has $50,000 and 400 m² of exterior surface for wall insulation ($120/m²; $9/m²/yr savings) or roof insulation ($80/m²; $7/m²/yr savings).
steps: Name the two design variables and units before writing coefficients.
Write the objective, both ≤ constraints, and nonnegative bounds.
Hand-check one feasible and one infeasible candidate against every constraint.
Predict the binding constraint(s); solve later and compare with that prediction.
slides.teaching: Expected formulation: x_wall and x_roof in m²; maximize 9x_wall + 7x_roof; x_wall + x_roof <= 400; 120x_wall + 80x_roof <= 50000; x>=0. Verified optimum (not required here): (400,0), $3,600/yr; surface binds and budget has slack. The hand-check makes formulation errors visible before linprog is allowed to declare success.

slides.title: Formulate first; solve and verify second
takeaways: Name variables, objective, constraints, and bounds—with units—before writing arrays.
If a finite LP optimum exists, at least one optimal extreme point exists; uniqueness is not guaranteed.
linprog reports a globally optimal numerical solution subject to feasibility and optimality tolerances.
Check success, residuals, constraints, and the real-world formulation before trusting the result.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students name, in one sentence, which two constraints bind at Radley Hall's optimal roof split, with the numbers.
